citation.title: Novel Artificial Neural Network Aided Structural Topology Optimization
citation.authors: Xiangrui Kong, Yuching Wu, Peng Zhu, Peng Zhi, Qianfan Yang
citation.venue: Applied Sciences 14(23) (2024) 11416 (MDPI; open access, CC BY 4.0; published 8 Dec 2024)
citation.version_coded: version of record, publisher PDF (30 pp.) from MDPI's file host (mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/applsci/applsci-14-11416/article_deploy/applsci-14-11416.pdf), read in full as text; pp. 13-15 and 18-19 also checked on the rendered pages, and the Table 1-3 values were read from the embedded table images at high zoom

included.reason: I-SPEED (screening code confirmed at full text; cost proxy = share of run time spent in FE analysis, SIMP vs the network-aided method, stated in the abstract)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: FE analysis takes over 90% of SIMP run time, but a smaller share in the partitioned-network method: 40% per the abstract, 17-65% across 60×60 to 480×480 meshes in Fig. 14. No absolute run times are reported.
claim.key_phrase: takes more than 90% of the total operation time of the SIMP method
claim.location: Abstract (§5.1 rule 1: quantitative comparison with SIMP); data in Sec. 5.4, Figs. 13-14, pp. 18-19
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Not derivable: only shares of run time are given, never absolute times for either method (Sec. 5.4, Figs. 13-14). SIMP FE share 90%, 96%, 99%, 99% at 60×60, 120×120, 240×240, 480×480 (Fig. 13); network method FE 17%, 27%, 61%, 65%, network inference 43%, 38%, 20%, 8%, other 40%, 35%, 19%, 27% (Fig. 14). The abstract's 40% matches no FE share in Fig. 14 (their mean is 42.5% [derived]); 40% is the share of the other modules at 60×60.
claim.alternatives: (1) Conclusion, quality: structural performance of the network and SIMP designs differs by less than 10%. (2) Tables 1-3, pp. 14-15 (unlabelled objective values, network vs SIMP, read from table images): L-beam 489.6 and 517.5 vs 487.4 (120×120, Np = 2 and 3), 433.3 and 422.2 vs 434.7 (240×240), 417.8 and 397.5 vs 428.2 (480×480); MBB 227.8 and 218.6 vs 225.3, 226.4 and 209.5 vs 223.8, 227.9 and 210.8 vs 226.7; column 16.7 and 16.1 vs 17.6, 17.5 and 16.4 vs 17.1, 18.2 and 17.4 vs 16.7 [derived range: -8.5% to +9.0% vs SIMP]. (3) Fig. 12, p. 13: SIMP and network objective histories nearly coincide over 50 iterations. (4) Abstract, qualitative: computational efficiency considerably improved.

baseline.classical_method: SIMP compliance minimization (penalty 3) with the optimality-criteria update and a density filter (Sec. 2.1); the network method replaces the fine-scale FE sensitivity computation with a partitioned CNN plus fully connected network fed by coarse-scale FE displacements and densities (Sec. 2-3)
baseline.solver: a sparse matrix equation solver, type not stated (Sec. 5.4)
baseline.problem_size: Timing study: 60×60, 120×120, 240×240 and 480×480 meshes, 3×3 partitions (Figs. 13-14) [derived: 7,442 to 462,722 nodal DOFs]; examples 60×60 to 240×960 (Sec. 4, Tables 1-6)
baseline.classical_iterations: 20 optimization iterations for every example (Sec. 4.1-4.5); Figs. 11-12 plot 50 iterations; Sec. 5.1 says most examples converge within 10 to 20 steps
baseline.classical_time: not stated in absolute terms; FE share of SIMP run time 90-99% (Fig. 13)
baseline.ml_time: not stated in absolute terms; shares only (Fig. 14)
baseline.training_time: not stated; loss curves over 100 training epochs, which the text calls generations (Sec. 3.3, Figs. 3-4)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated clearly: training data are SIMP runs on random boundary conditions and volume fractions (Sec. 3.2), dataset size not stated; Sec. 3.3 gives about 30 min for a process of generating randomly partitioned TO iterations, without saying what it includes
baseline.quality_metric: Unlabelled objective value of the final designs, network vs SIMP (bar charts in Tables 1-6; compliance inferred); objective histories (Figs. 11-12); density difference map (Fig. 5b)
baseline.quality_gap: Network designs within about ±9% of the SIMP objective across Tables 1-3 [derived], lower than SIMP in 10 of 18 cases [derived]; the conclusion states less than 10%. Volume fractions of the network designs are not reported

R1.evidence: Sec. 4-5: the cost claim rests on shares of run time (Figs. 13-14) with no absolute times, and the timed runs are not linked to a stated design case [the 3×3-partition L-beams of Table 1 inferred]. Quality is reported separately as unlabelled objective values within about ±9% of SIMP (Tables 1-3 [derived]); volume fractions are not reported, and SIMP stops after a fixed 20 iterations. Matching is therefore loose. A stricter reading (no measured speed at all) gives fail.

R2.evidence: Sec. 2.1, 4 and 5.4: the SIMP implementation, solver type and hardware are not stated, and no absolute time exists, so (a), (b), (c) and (e) cannot be derived. (d) is not established: SIMP uses 20 iterations while most examples converge within 10 to 20 steps (Sec. 5.1), and both methods share the budget. An FE share of 90-99% is typical of SIMP codes whose cost is dominated by the linear solve, so no inefficiency is evident [inferred]. Unsure, so pass.

R3.evidence: The network is trained offline on random SIMP runs and reused across examples (Sec. 3.2; Conclusion) [reuse inferred]. Training time, dataset size and break-even are not reported; the only cost figure is about 30 min for a process of generating randomly partitioned TO iterations (Sec. 3.3), which may be the data-generation cost [inferred]. The efficiency claim covers the whole design process (abstract), not per-query inference. If the 30 min is not read as a data cost, R3 = fail (R3-no-cost).

R4.evidence: Tables 1-6: an objective value is given for every network and SIMP design, presumably from FE analysis of the returned design [inferred; the quantity and its computation are not stated]. Volume fractions and constraint satisfaction of the network designs are not reported, and disconnections or failed runs are not counted; the 25 Appendix A cases show images only.

reporting.n_test_cases: 5 examples (Sec. 4); Tables 1-3: 3 meshes × 2 partition numbers for the L-beam, MBB beam and column; Tables 4-6: volume fraction × filter radius grids for the same three structures; Appendix A: 25 further structures (images only); time shares for 4 mesh sizes (Figs. 13-14)

notes: Screening code was I-SPEED; kept. The screening rationale says the networks map boundary and mesh conditions to density; the full text shows that they predict fine-scale sensitivities inside SIMP from coarse-scale FE displacements (Sec. 2.3, 3), so method_family is coded cnn (CNN plus fully connected network). Stratum judgment: the abstract's only quantitative classical comparison is a share of run time, which is taken as a cost proxy under §5.1 rule 1; it cannot show a speed-up by itself, because the network adds its own inference time (8-43% of the run, Fig. 14) and no absolute times are given. If the verifier rejects the proxy, the next candidate is the conclusion's quality statement (less than 10% difference), i.e., stratum Q. Access: www.mdpi.com returned HTTP 403 (Access Denied) to curl and to WebFetch; the PDF came from MDPI's own file host, the same publisher copy (CC BY 4.0); no challenge was involved. Internal inconsistencies: the abstract's 40% FE share matches no FE share in Fig. 14; Sec. 4 sets 20 iterations while Figs. 11-12 plot 50; the MBB mesh is 360×120 in Sec. 4.2 but 320×120 in the Table 5 caption; in 10 of 18 Table 1-3 cases the network design has a lower objective than SIMP [derived], which at equal volume suggests an unconverged 20-iteration SIMP reference or volume differences [inferred]. Editorial flags for the verifier: the introduction discusses network-topology and game-model optimization, Sec. 2 contains leftover journal-template instructions about data deposition, and Sec. 5 opens with generic advice on comparing multi-objective metaheuristics that is not applied. Data statement: contributions are in the article; further inquiries go to the corresponding authors. No code statement. retest_candidate false: no public code. No author named Jun Wang.
